title: Why Handover Matters Between Housekeeping Shifts
excerpt: A good housekeeping handover transfers unfinished work, exceptions, hazards, access issues and priorities so the incoming shift can continue safely without guessing.
content_html:
Housekeeping does not stop neatly at a shift boundary. Rooms may still be drying, supplies may be low, equipment may be unavailable and priority tasks may remain open. A shift handover makes that changing situation visible to the incoming team so work can continue without relying on guesswork.

Handover is about continuity

HSE describes effective shift handover as the reliable transfer of task-relevant information when responsibility moves from one person or team to another. The same principle applies to housekeeping: the incoming shift needs enough accurate information to understand what has been completed, what remains and what has changed.

What the next shift needs to know

  • Outstanding tasks: work that is incomplete, deferred or waiting for access.
  • Exceptions: unusual soil, spills, damage, complaints or areas that did not meet the normal standard.
  • Safety and access: wet floors, isolated areas, maintenance activity, locked rooms or other restrictions.
  • Equipment and supplies: machines out of service, low stock, missing tools or items waiting for reprocessing.
  • Priority changes: events, occupancy changes, room turnover or instructions that alter the normal sequence.

Use verbal and written handover together

HSE recommends handover that is two-way and supported by both verbal and written communication. A short conversation lets the incoming team ask questions; a log or digital record provides a reference after the outgoing team has left. One should support the other rather than replace it.

A simple housekeeping handover structure

  1. Prepare: the outgoing shift reviews open work and records exceptions before changeover.
  2. Transfer: both shifts discuss priorities, hazards, access issues and incomplete tasks.
  3. Cross-check: the incoming shift confirms what it has understood and checks critical areas or records where needed.
  4. Accept responsibility: ownership of the open work becomes clear at the end of handover.

Record exceptions, not unnecessary noise

A handover should not become a second copy of the entire cleaning schedule. The schedule already defines routine work. Handover is most useful when it highlights what the next shift would not know from the normal plan: incomplete work, unusual conditions, changed priorities and unresolved problems.

Connect handover to checklists and logs

CDC environmental-cleaning guidance uses schedules, checklists, logs and job aids to support consistent work. In a housekeeping system, completion records show what was due and done; handover records explain what changed, what failed or what still needs attention.

Common handover failures

  • Assuming the next shift will notice unfinished work.
  • Using vague notes such as “check area” without describing the issue.
  • Reporting a problem without assigning or accepting follow-up responsibility.
  • Passing on a verbal message that is not recorded when the issue will outlast the conversation.
  • Filling the handover with routine information so important exceptions are difficult to find.

Practical takeaway

A useful handover answers three questions: What changed? What is still open? What does the next shift need to act on first? Keep the information concise, specific and easy to cross-check.

References

  1. HSE — Shift handover.
  2. CDC — Environmental Cleaning Procedures.
